Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 57
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Architect
  trauma_type: Trauma to a loved one
  pcl5: 70

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Spatial Triggers: Physical locations, Auditory (Language Confusion): Incomprehensible chatter, Olfactory (Hospital): Hospital or antiseptic smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Friends: avoid seeing friends, Compulsive Exercise: I push myself to exercise excessively, Avoid Medical Cues: Hospitals/ Ambulances/ Physical Examinations
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Faith: I have lost my faith in people, life, or a higher power, Exposed to Others: I feel that others can see what happened to me just by looking at me, Lost Meaning: Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore

Vignette:
Aroha was fifty-seven when she finally booked the appointment, her hand lingering on the clinic’s automatic door long before she pushed through. Five years earlier, the sudden collapse of her brother had drawn her into a space that would later dictate the contours of her days. She remembered the exact corridor where the sliding glass doors sealed him away, the heavy antiseptic scent meeting her face the moment she entered, and the rapid, overlapping voices of nurses and residents that had blurred into an incomprehensible chatter. In that suspended moment, her faith in bodies and in the careful hands that tended them had fractured. She had come to believe that illness could arrive without warning and that the people charged with guarding health were no safer to trust than anyone else. In the months that followed, the physical geography of the hospital had bled into her wider world. Aroha found herself navigating a city that suddenly felt too vast and too familiar at once. Every clinical building, every waiting room with its identical vinyl chairs, every doorway with its automatic sweep became a spatial reminder of that corridor. What frightened her most was the certainty that others could see the rupture in her, that the shock of those early weeks was still written across her face for anyone to read. She felt exposed in staffed offices, even in the drafting room of her architecture practice, where the fluorescent lights and the sharp angles of suspended ceilings mirrored the hospital’s layout. When clients spoke to her, their words often seemed to slip past her like that early stream of medical chatter, and she would nod politely while her attention remained anchored to the smell of floor wax or the distant hum of the building’s ventilation system. Her days took on a quiet rhythm of avoidance. She stopped returning calls from her sister and declined invitations to neighborhood dinners. She told herself the studio demanded her time. Alongside this, she committed herself to an exhaustive exercise routine, pushing her body through long, solitary runs and relentless weight sessions, her muscles aching with the exertion. She avoided medical cues with a practiced precision: she scheduled dental cleanings early in the morning to sidestep the clinic’s chemical cleaners, declined routine blood work, and turned her head when an ambulance passed the practice window. These habits formed steadily over weeks and months, each one carving out space while she remained present but increasingly distant. Her colleagues noticed the shift. She missed the unveiling of a major commission as she spent the evening pacing the studio’s open-plan floor, watching the sunset rather than greeting the assembled team. Nothing in her life felt particularly meaningful anymore; the blueprints she drew and the buildings she walked through seemed to belong to a world that had moved on without her. Her PCL-5 score of 70 mirrored this lived reality, capturing the weight of days spent braced against invisible reminders. The decision to seek help arrived not as a sudden revelation but as a quiet accumulation. Divorced and managing a practice that had grown quieter with her absence, Aroha realized that her legs no longer carried her where she wanted to go. The hospital scent of a new hand sanitizer bottle on her desk was enough to make her breath catch, and the memory of that corridor’s spatial boundaries still pulled her back. She came to therapy hoping to find a way to stand in a room without feeling transparent, to trust that the ground would hold, and to stop pushing herself so relentlessly toward a horizon that kept receding. She did not expect the past to vanish, only to stop dictating every step.
